utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could I remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we please go into private session. Various matters that would reveal the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I repeat, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. You will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions that are to be asked of you in this trial. The Chamber would like to thank you for the assistance that you've given and your attendance here, and you are of course now free to go back to your home and your other interests. So thank you indeed. The court officer will show you out. If you wait just a moment, we will close the shutters while you leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Our next witness is Ivan Grujic and I'd would like to call him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to -- there's a binder of materials which I think have been provided to the Defence -- and in hard copy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please move closer to the microphone for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll move in a little closer, Your Honour. Binders have been distributed to Defence counsel, and I will ask that they be distributed to Your Honours and the registry officials. They relate to the documents that will be tendered through the witness today. The documents will also be tendered in e-court. The purpose of the binder is to keep things as efficient as possible. There are a large amount of documents that won't be in the binder but an index to those documents are at the front. And we would be tendering those documents in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grujic. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you please state your full name and your position at the moment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Ivan Grujic. Currently I'm employed as assistant minister in the Ministry for the families -- for Families, Defenders and Intergenerational Solidarity in the office for missing persons. I am also the president of the governmental commission for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In your capacity in this position, were you asked to prepare a report by the Office of the Prosecutor for the Milosevic case in relation to your administration's activities dealing with missing and detained people as well as in relation to the findings you made on the basis of your records?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Pursuant to a request of the ICTY, I compiled such a report and submitted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to that report, did you testify in the Milosevic case as an expert witness in March 2003?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And subsequently in the -- and subsequently in the Martic case this year, did you testify as an expert witness and also prepare an updated report from 2003 in relation to the same matters?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I have distributed a binder of materials, of which you have a copy. And I would ask that you turn to tab 1.2, please. Or 1.1. And the ERN number is 0468-7742 to 0468-7757. Is this a copy of your updated report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Complete, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that report. The 2003 report was submitted later last year, but a copy of the updated report was provided to the Defence early last week, and it's updated only in a few minor areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 530, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I also seek to tender, Your Honour, some attachments to that report, and the first attachment can be found at tab 1.2, and it's a decree on the establishment and work of a commission for tracing persons missing in the war operations in the Republic of Croatia. The B/C/S number is 0117-6631 to 6633. This is an attachment referred to in the witness's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 531, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I also seek to tender at tab 1.3, this is an attachment 2.f. to the witness's report, it's the Decree on the Internal Organisation of the Ministry of Family, Defenders and Intergenerational Solidarity Administration for Detained and Missing Persons. The ERN number is 0469-0799 to 0469-0802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will be Exhibit 532.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I also seek to tender at tab 1.4, this is attachment A to the report, and it's entitled Republic of Croatia, government decision to form the Republic of Croatia government commission for detained and missing persons. And the ERN number is 0469-0796 to 0469-0798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 533, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I also seek to tender at tab 1.5, this is attachment 14A to the expert report. This is an organigramme of those taking part in exhumations. The B/C/S number is 0469-6078, 0469-6079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 534, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I also seek to tender tab 1.6, which is attachment 6.a. This is the Commission for Detained and Missing Persons, copy of questionnaire on missing persons. The B/C/S ERN number is 0469-3240 to 0469-3251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 535, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I also seek to tender the transcript of this witness in the Milosevic case dated the 3rd to the 4th of March, 2003. The ERN number is one complete range, 0504-5454 to 0504-5591.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 536, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we commence with the witness, I would ask that the witness be allowed to use the binder which he has, which is slightly different to Your Honours' and Defence counsel in the sense that it contains annotations and notes which he has made to prepare himself for this testimony. It will be -- the binder can be available for review at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Are you not wanting it tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Not to tender, it's just working notes that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. It won't be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, I would like to ask you some aspects -- about some particular aspects of the report that you have written and firstly in relation to your qualifications, your educational qualifications. Can you briefly explain what post-secondary education you have had in your career?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I am a graduate criminologist, and I also have a degree in traffic engineering. Of course I have also passed the exam to work in government administration, and I have a certificate from the Ministry of the Interior. All this is in my statement. The entire chronology of my training and education and professional degrees is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the statement you refer to some specialist police training that you had undertaken while serving with the Ministry of the Interior. Can you briefly explain what that specialist police training was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: This was intelligence and counter-intelligence training in the Ministry of the Interior. That was a one-year course which I mentioned right away, and at the end of it I received a diploma.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also state your work experience in your expert report. But in brief summary can you state your work experience?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, from 1972 I worked in the police, and I worked on almost all the jobs that exist in the police. I was a policeman on the beat, I was a clerk, I was an inspector, I was an independent inspector in charge of a whole police unit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, police station.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: -- during the war. Then I was transferred to the Ministry of Defence where I did the same work until 1993 when, by a decision of the government, I was appointed president of the commission for missing persons. From 1993 onwards, I have been dealing exclusively with issues of missing persons. From 1993 until today, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in addition to missing persons, also in relation to detained persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: This is linked. There are two ways one can find a missing person. One can find a missing person alive, because for whatever reason they lost contact with their family, but we managed to find that person; or we find that the person is a prisoner and then we take measures to have the person released. On the other hand, a missing person can be found dead. In that case, one has to establish where the corpse is, exhume it, identify it, and confirm that this is the missing person in question. In that case, the missing person is removed from the list of missing persons being sought. Therefore, an investigation is conducted into the fate of every missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to your first employment with the commission for detainees and missing persons in 1993, you have stated that you were made president of that commission. Can you give a brief description of how that commission has evolved over time from that date, 1993, to 2006? And also can you give a brief summary of what preceded that commission prior to 1993 in terms of those types of activities? It's in your statement, but just if you can briefly summarise.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to present this very briefly. In 1991 the government of the Republic of Croatia realised that in the Republic of Croatia there are 18.000 missing persons recorded in Croatia. Pursuant to its positive legislation, it decided to create an administrative body to attempt to deal with this problem. In 1991 the commission for searching for missing persons was established. Its main task was to gather and process information about civilian and other victims and missing persons from the territory of the Republic of Croatia. That is the definition. As it was observed that the information was in a state of chaos, more or less, on the 13th of May, 1993, the government decided to establish a governmental commission which would be directly responsible to the government, and I was appointed head of that commission. The commission had three main lines of activity: The exchange of prisoners; supervision of the treatment and accommodation of prisoners of war; and gathering and processing information about missing persons. As the government administration developed, there were internal changes, and in the year 2000 this commission grew into a government bureau for prisoners and missing persons. Its tasks were identical to those of the commission, and the government again appointed me head of that office. As the government administration developed further and was reorganised in 2004, the office of the government stopped its work and an administration for prisoners and missing persons was established within the Ministry for the Family, Defenders and Intergenerational Solidarity, and I was appointed assistant minister. As it was observed that there were certain problems arising due to coordination between the different ministries, because more than one ministry is involved in this task, the cabinet decided to establish, in parallel with this administration, also a commission of the government of Croatia, as an interministry body, and after this commission was established I was appointed its president. I was the president of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. So in short, for the last 13 years you have been concentrating your professional career on the location of missing people and the identification of detained people, et cetera. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. In every form of organisation from 1993 to date, I have headed government bodies dealing with the search for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as part of that role in your report you referred to your commission or administration's involvement in the supervision and the conduct of exhumations in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Not only the supervision of the exhumations, but the commission or the body dealing with this in 1993 primarily organised the exhumation but also kept records pertaining to the exhumations. These were two sets of records. One was the record of mortal remains, and the other were records of identification of these mortal remains. These were two sets of records maintained by the government administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you stated earlier that prior to 1993 there was a commission for missing people, and then also in your report you state there was a commission for captured -- captured people in the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That is correct. As I said, in 1991 a commission for searching for missing persons in the war activities in the Republic of Croatia was established, but also a commission was established to look into the treatment of prisoners taken during armed clashes. These two were joined together in the government commission that was established in 1993, or the government office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the mandate of the -- those two commissions and then subsequently in 1993 the one commission and the mandate of your administration now, is it only in relation to detained and missing people arising out of the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And briefly can you state to the court the period of time the conflict ensued in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: According to the records we have, there are several categories of suffering or casualties we will discuss. In the -- in January 1991 the first cases were recorded of victims. The greatest intensity was after June, increasing in September and culminating in December 1991. And then it went on until May 1992 at a somewhat lower intensity. So this went on until mid-1992. Of course after this we have records of missing persons, but much less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did military operations of any sort finish in Croatia? What's the end point of the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The end came in 1995 when military and police operations were undertaken to liberate the occupied territories, and that was when armed conflict practically ceased. But until the end of the peaceful reintegration of the Croatian Danube region, which occurred in 1998, we have records of individual deaths and missing persons. Or rather, no, not missing persons, I apologise, but displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Croatian Danube region, that includes Vukovar and Eastern Slavonia; is that correct? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Danube region or the Podunavlje is the area through which the River Danube flows. That refers to Baranja and part of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Just briefly can you explain the commission's activities whilst the conflict was occurring in Croatia, say from 1991 to 1995, compared to the commission's or the administration's activities after 1995 in relation to detained and missing people?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: With respect to missing and detained persons, there is a continuity in the search, but the activities undertaken change. In 1991 until 1993 or 1994, the major method of dealing with these cases was release of prisoners from camps and prisons. This was done through negotiations with the opposite side or with those in whose power the detainees were, in cooperation with the ICRC. And exchanges were carried out and the prisoners released. Most of these prisoners were released by 1994. It then became apparent that the remaining missing persons would unfortunately most likely be found in mass graves, and ultimately this proved to be correct. In 1996, therefore -- excuse me, 1995, a team was formed to conduct exhumations, and they began to conduct exhumations in the previously occupied areas of Croatia. 142 mass graves were found, and in this way we began to find missing persons. Therefore, the method of finding or the way in which these persons were found changed and records were kept in the administration, depending on the methods used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And why were exhumation teams on an exhumation team only formed in 1995 and not before that? Did anything prevent that from happening?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, earlier on such teams were not necessary. It was quite obvious that all the mass graves hitherto found had come into existence in the temporarily occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia. This is when the need arose to set up a team like that and to start the exhumations. Needless to say, for as long as the areas were under occupation our own teams, teams under the administration of the Republic of Croatia were not able to reach these areas, were not allowed into these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And that exhumation process, is that still continuing until the current time, until now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As we speak, another exhumation is getting off the ground in Eastern Slavonia where the ground is being probed for mass graves. Some mortal remains have been observed in the village of Karadzicevo, and all this means is that the exhumations are continuing. We are collecting information on other possible mass grave sites, as there is still a long list of missing persons. Our hope is that we will be able to find most of these remaining missing persons in places like these.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to the commission and the administration's activities in relation to detained people. In your report you state that 7.666 people were detained during the conflict or the aggression against Croatia. And you state that 5.013 were of Croat ethnicity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Since 1991 and all the way until the last operations of liberating the Croatian territories, 7.666 people were set free who had been detained in Serbia, Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as in temporarily occupied territories of Croatia itself. The last exchange of this type occurred on the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the records you used to come to that figure, can you explain briefly what those records are, to be able to arrive at that figure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: All these prisoners were tracked down based on a variety of sources. First of all, there were the exchange lists that were made wherever an exchange took place. And these lists were made before the first commission back in 1991 was ever set up because there were local exchanges that were organised, so to speak, at local levels. Then you had the lists produced by the exchange commission. There was information as well recorded by the ICRC in prisons and camps. These were the principal sources for our own files and records. There are certain limitations, obviously, to this method. In 1991 we had wartime conditions, and the administration had not yet been set up properly. Records were made and kept in the only way that was available to us at the time. Aside from that, I must add that the documentation is being added to on a permanent basis. Whenever a former POW needs a document to certify their previous status as such, information is retrieved directly from this person and the person is normally requested to provide a statement. In addition to that, most of those prisoners have undergone medical checks, and once they are released usually there are documents to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you had access to that documentation to come up with that figure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The documentation is an integral part of the archive, of which I am head. It is precisely based on this archive that lists were drawn up, records are kept and permanently updated. Therefore, these records change over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you give us an approximate size of the volume of those records in relation to coming to that figure of 7.666, what amount of documentation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost each detainee has his or her own medical history containing all the information that we have. Most of this information has been processed electronically, which means that we have 7.666 files, personal files. Aside from that, there are documents existing in most cases showing how the exchanges occurred and what exactly was done. This is a massive amount of documents. That's as specific as I can be. So much for any documents concerning detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we now can move to the figure that you provide in relation to missing people in relation to Croatia as a whole, currently you list that there's 1140 people that are still recorded as missing in Croatia as a result of the conflict, and 991 of those people are of Croat ethnicity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I must make a correction there. Perhaps it was a mistranslation or perhaps I misheard. I'm talking about 1.140 missing persons. Based on information provided by their families, 991 of those are ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And what -- what are the sources of your -- what documentation is used to source that figure? Can you describe the type of documentation that's used?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: In order to arrive at this figure we used questionnaires on missing persons. This means that a questionnaire was completed in relation to each and every missing person covering a lot of ground. This means that each missing person has a file, and the person who initiated this procedure to track the missing person down is recorded, the person's name. This is in keeping with the international procedures that are in place in cases like these, as well as those used by the International Red Cross, except that we try to cover a lot more ground and include as most [as interpreted] information as possible on our missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also state in your report that in 1994 that's when the major campaign was conducted in order to have people report anyone that was missing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Perhaps I can say a few words about this. In 1993 information on missing persons was scarce and insufficient to start a proper search. The Croatian government received a proposal for renewing this request to track down these missing persons. We tried to do the best we could. So the first step we took is -- was to enlist the help of the experts, of computer experts, psychologists and other experts to produce a questionnaire for us, including questions based on which we could pursue our leads, and this is how the questionnaire was created, the questionnaire to track down missing persons. After that we started training staff who would work on this, who would gather information. At the same time there was a media campaign to encourage families to report their own missing persons, and this campaign was conducted both in the printed media and on TV. After that information was gathered in 102 Croatian Red Cross offices, in Consulates across the Republic of Croatia, so these were the places where information was being gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujic. That gives us a brief understanding of it. This is explained in much detail in your report. So perhaps maybe if we can move to the figure of people that were reported missing in 1994 after this campaign was conducted. And in your report you state that 3.052 people were reported missing and of that number, 2.709 were of Croat ethnicity. Now this is back in 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's right. We started this campaign and that was the figure that we arrived at. This meant that we were successful in gathering information on more or less all the missing persons that we knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just briefly, as of this date you state that there are still 1140 people recorded as missing in Croatia, or that were living in Croatia. Approximately that 2.000 people that have since been found from 1994 to 2006, have most of them been found alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Dead, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the missing person report, you attached one of those to your statement, is that correct, a blank missing person report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think each report contains about six or seven pages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: More, I think. I think each report contains 12 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And also when a missing person was reported, say back in 1994, were also other documentation attached to that missing person report to assist you in your process of trying to find them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As for these questionnaires, the total number of pages is about 12.500 pages. Plus the documents. We asked each and every family, which you can see in the statement, to provide whatever documents they thought might be helpful in tracking down a missing person. As a result we received photographs, medical files, dental records, records of any previous injuries and a whole series of other documents that families believed might prove helpful in our search. Therefore, in addition to the initial documents, also these family files or documents obtained from families were then added to each file.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that documentation, is that kept at your administration?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's part of the archive of the administration of which I am head. The questionnaires have been processed electronically, but we also keep hard copies of each and every document and questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now move to exhumations conducted and identifications conducted as a result of them. You state in your report that 3.568 people have been exhumed to this date and 2.982 have been identified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And of the 2.597 that have been identified -- sorry, that's my mistake. Of the 2.982 that have been identified, you state that 2.597 are of Croat ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. This is information provided by families as bodies were identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just to be clear, these exhumations only relate to death arising out of the effects of the conflict as opposed to any other natural causes during that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's quite correct. These are mass graves, and victims were found inside these mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, does that figure of 3.568, does that just relate to mass graves in Croatia, or does it relate to Croatian victims that were exhumed in other states as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: This refers to victims exhumed in the Republic of Croatia, the Croatian territories that were previously occupied, and that's the only thing that these figures refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps if we can take one example of the type of documentation that would be present for a person that was exhumed and subsequently identified. What type of documentation would we expect to see if we wanted to look into one particular case?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, there is an order from the relevant district court to start an exhumation. These orders are part of our documentation. In addition to this, there are records of the exhumation, there are photo files that are made on the spot, there are lists of those involved in the exhumation, and a brief report on the number of victims found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Also would there be autopsy reports for each of the victims exhumed, or only for some of them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: For each. Each time a body is exhumed there is a procedure that is applied, and each victim has a file containing every step that was taken with the body. The next step is identifying the body. If there is a positive ID, then a certificate of death and a finding concerning the cause of death is added to the person's file, as well as any results of DNA analysis, if that was how the body was eventually identified. So all these go into the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the files in relation to those exhumed and identified, where are they kept? Are they kept together in one place or in a number of places?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: All these documents are kept in the administration, in our office. In addition to this, the file about the processing of mortal remains is copied and sent to the Institute for Forensic Medicine. They also send feedback to us, the same sort of information, because the government says that we are the relevant body for exhumations and identifying bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can just give us an idea of the volume of material that would relate to, say, one person that's been exhumed and identified, perhaps in the terms of numbers of pages that would be related to each individual, can you give us an approximate figure of how many pages that would be?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: This would average about 10 pages in relation to each individual. If you include the photographic files, then this adds up to a lot more, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to data compilation, compiling data, as you have done in your expert report to be able to come up with these figures, and in relation to record-keeping and analysis, in your experience -- what has been your experience in the commission since 1993 in relation to these activities, either your involvement in them or the involvement of members of your staff? Can you explain the type of experience that you may or may not have had in being able to compile these types of figures?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: As I've already pointed out, our administration is in charge of keeping official records. All the data have been processed electronically. Of course we are able to provide statistics on any information that is in our possession. Wherever necessary, we can access our data files and we can complement our previous findings, especially in cases where information is not 100 per cent reliable, but, rather, evaluations are drawn up or assessments are made, analysis conducted, based on such information as happens to be in our possession. All the information that I have provided here, based on our own files, is derived from our files. I was personally involved, and I also supervised some of my staff working on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to your staff, about how many staff work in the administration at the moment, dealing with detainees and missing persons, on a full-time basis?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Another five persons are busy doing this in our administration. But I am talking about an administration which is also charged with organising this. When you have an exhumation, when bodies are identified, we enlist the assistance of a large number of other experts, experts from other ministries. From other relevant ministries, I should add. We, the administration, are the coordinating body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the results of your findings of this Croatia-wide analysis in your report, the people that put those findings or results together, did that include you and other members of this staff of five people that you talk about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with the qualifications of these people that were assisting in putting this data together, do you feel that they were qualified enough to be able to put this data together accurately?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is their fundamental task. Let me try to clarify this. The person in charge of the missing persons files in my administration has access to all information and is authorised to access any file. That is that person's job, that's why that person receives his or her salary, and that applies to everything we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This may be an appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We must now have the first adjournment. It will be necessary for it to be a half hour. And it will mean we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, before the break we discussed the figures that you have arrived at in your report about the effects of the conflict on detained, missing and exhumed people in Croatia. I'd now like to turn to the figure that you arrive at in relation to the number of people killed in the conflict. And in that report you state that there was 12.078 people killed, and 7.012 were of Croat ethnicity, and then there were 4.179 of unknown ethnicity, and then you state some further smaller numbers in relation to other ethnic groups. The question I ask you is: How did you arrive at that figure of people killed, and what types of documentation did you use or have access to to support that figure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: In the year 2002, the government of the Republic of Croatia entrusted to my administration the task of making a provisional list - and I emphasise a provisional list - of persons killed in the Republic of Croatia. The previous lists were not very good. In order to achieve a unified provisional list, we used the lists of the Ministry of Health and the lists of the Ministry of Family, Defenders and Intergenerational Solidarity. The former referred -- or, rather, the latter referred to civilians, and the former to members of the armed forces. By collating these lists, we arrived at the figure we have here today. We added to those two lists persons exhumed and identified and recorded in our administration, so that three lists were actually used to generate this list, and it's a list subject to change. This list has its limitations. You yourself have noted that the ethnic make-up is provided for only about two-thirds of these persons. That's because a lot of data is missing. And the remaining information has yet to be collected in order to achieve the best possible results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Ministry of Health list, are you saying that relates to civilians or to members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: This relates to civilians for the most part. They made this list by obtaining names and -- first and last names from the ground, from the Vukovar area and other occupied areas during the conflict. They could not get good quality information. It was only first and last names without other details. That's what could be done at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And Ministry of Health list, do you have the underlying documentation that was used to come up with that Ministry of Health list, or do you just have the Ministry of Health list?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: No, we don't have the underlying documentation. This task involved employees of the Ministry of Health working on this issue. That is a department called the department for information and investigation. They provided us a list containing all the parameters they had at their disposal about each person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the list provided by the Ministry of Family, Defenders and Intergenerational Solidarity, that list, do you have that at your administration?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: No. This information was of the same kind as the information obtained from the Ministry of Health. But this was done within the ministry of which my administration is a part, and the information is there in the ministry because their families achieved their rights and benefits through this ministry, and therefore the information is more complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that the three lists from the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Family, Defenders and Intergenerational Solidarity and your information in relation to those exhumed and identified, the results of those lists were combined and put together, and that's how you determined the figure in this report of the numbers killed in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. These three lists were put together, so this is a result of these three lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the figure of displaced people that you state were displaced as a result of the conflict in Croatia, in your report you state that 230.338 were displaced and of that, of that number, 205.215 were of Croatian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the official information of the administration dealing with these issues, the total number of displaced is to 230.338, and of these, 205.215 are of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in the English translation of your report the word "displaced" is used. When this term "displaced" is used, can you describe further whether these people were displaced of their own choice or displaced by force? How do you use that word "displaced"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The word in Croatian is "expellee," and this can be seen in the file. This means that they left their residence by force, and that they were accommodated within the country in which they were expelled from their homes. The other category is that of refugees, and those are persons who were outside the Republic of Croatia. These are the two categories covered by the two different terms, "displaced" and "refugees."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And what documentation did you use to arrive at that figure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: When information is gathered about missing persons, there is a questionnaire whether -- we ask whether the family of the missing person is displaced or not. And other information is sought from the administration for displaced persons and refugees, and they gave us the official data I have presented here. This data is public, it is published.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the data that the administration for displaced persons and refugees gave you, did they give you the documentation on which their figure was based or did they just give you the figure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: No, they just forwarded to us the documents, numbers and statistics. It would have not have been possible for them to forward all the details because, as you can see, it's 200.000 files and supporting materials with these. And this would amount to half a million documents, and you can't forward that volume, it wouldn't be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say 200.000 files, that's an approximate figure. Are you stating that for each of the displaced people or each of the expelled people in Croatia then there is a file on each one of them? And I'm referring to the figure of 230.338.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: 220.338, that's the correct number. Each of these persons, each of these 220.338, had their personal file of a displaced person, including the time and circumstances in which they were expelled from their home, the temporary accommodation provided by the state, the donations provided by the state for their survival, everything concerning their status. All of this is contained in their file. There is a file to support each person contained in this figure. That's absolutely true. Each person has a file.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. I misquoted the number. You're right, it's 220.338 in your report. Have you seen one of those files?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, of course. One should know that the administration for displaced persons is an integral part of the state administration, just as my administration is, and we are in constant contact, exchanging information, because most of the families of missing persons are displaced persons. So this is a kind of double victimisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But in relation to the files kept by the administration for refugees, about how many pages would they have on each individual -- on each expelled person? How many pages would be in each file, approximately?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The fundamental document is the two-page questionnaire. In addition to that, they have a number of various documents showing their revenues, decisions on their accommodation, and so on and so forth. So there are a number of additional documents. But the basis for the statistics, that is the two-page questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Grujic, in relation to your report it's perhaps sometimes unclear whether or not the results in relation to expelled, missing, detained, killed, exhumed, relate to the total figure of those people in the conflict in Croatia or whether or not those figures largely refer to, as you state in your report in a number of places, the aggression against the State of Croatia. And in further places in your report you refer to access to exhumation sites was gained after the liberation of previously occupied areas of the Republic of Croatia. I would just like to ask you some questions about this aggression against the State of Croatia, because you seem to relate a number of your figures to that activity, and I'm referring to certainly your figure of displaced people and your figure of killed people. You relate that to this aggression. So I'm going to ask you a series of questions about that so that we can put these figures in some sort of context. When you refer to the aggression against the State of Croatia, can you state when this aggression commenced and when it ceased? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The law on Croatian defenders defines this as the period from the 5th of August, 1990 to the 30th of June, 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the last year.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: We can go category by category and say that the first missing person, I'm referring to our official facts now, the first such person was recorded on the 10th of April, 1991. The first prisoner was recorded on the 23rd of January, 1991. The first person killed was recorded on the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That is, therefore, the period from the beginning of 1991. It grew in intensity and culminated between July when Baranja was occupied and part of Slavonia, and the 1st of May, 1992. That was the period of the greatest victimisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. It was unclear from the -- from your answer whether or not this -- you stated that the -- under the law, under the Croatian law whether or not it was stated that the aggression finished on the 30th of June, 1996. Was that the correct year?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That refers to the possible consequences caused for people because of the aggression. Yes, that is the last date under which the law gives people rights they can claim as a result of the aggression. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And based on your records that you have available to you in your office, can you just briefly state the areas in Croatia where this aggression occurred? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Based on the documentation I have available, and not based on my personal observation, one-third of the Republic of Croatia, approximately, was occupied. Its eastern part was occupied encompassing Baranja, Eastern Slavonia and part of Srijem. That is the Danube region. Then Western Slavonia was occupied, the Banovina area, Lika, stretching all the way to the Dalmatian hinterland, as well as the hinterland of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, to put these figures in context, briefly, very briefly, can you state what form this aggression took?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: This was armed aggression, leading to casualties, leading to people being expelled from their homes. People being killed, either due to artillery fire or direct fire. People being taken off to prison camps and prisons. And these were a single system in Serbia and Montenegro, and in the occupied areas, as well as in Bosnia. In this area many people went missing. As I said, in 1994, when many of the problems had been solved, there were 3.052 left, and today we are still looking for 1.140 persons. However, looking at it by area, everything I am mentioning, killed, expelled, imprisoned, missing, 50 per cent of these figures relate to the Danube region, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the same brief fashion, from your records can you describe who were the aggressors and who were the occupiers of this area? In very brief terms, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The occupation was carried out by members of paramilitary units and the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the paramilitary units, are you able to say what the ethnic composition, in the main, of those units were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I cannot say of what ethnicity they were, because I don't have this data. But it's evident that they were members of paramilitary formations bearing various names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can state those names briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I can recall several of them now. Arkan's men, the Red Berets, the White Eagles. Those are the names I can recall now. The milicija, Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. From your records -- you have just described who were the aggressors in relation to your report, but can you state who caused in general terms the expulsion, killing and detention during this aggression in Croatia? Are you saying that it's the same group as the aggressors that you just referred to or some other group or groups?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this witness is being asked to give a response which goes beyond his expertise and the topic of his testimony. We have had various other experts as well as witnesses who could testify directly about the political context. This witness should not be asked such questions because, if he is, many areas for cross-examination which will be opened up, which are not actually the subject of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has access to, as you are aware, large amount of records relating to the activity of the displacement, the expulsion, the killing, et cetera. And that's central to his report. All I'm asking is a question as to, from his information that he has received, not his own opinion, who was responsible for those activities on the basis of the reports and the documentation that he's received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, it's one thing for this man from his work and expertise to say these things have been discovered, this is what they disclose and what we have found about deaths and so forth and who is missing. You are now asking him, as Mr. Lukic says, to go into, I anticipate, the political situation and/or the military situation, which is something a good distance, I would have thought, from the primary basis of his work and his experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In terms of going to it in detail, that's not the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yeah, but why do you need it in general? How is it going to help us? We might ask a range of people to come and answer that question, and they would give us a great variety of answers of not a great deal of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. The only thing I can say in response is that Mr. Grujic is a witness that is coming here to provide evidence of the records that he has, and in those records this type of information is contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We think that the concern of Mr. Lukic is well-founded, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, perhaps if we can go back to the individuals that are referred to in your report, the ones that have been expelled, killed, missing, detained, are you able to say what the -- whether there was a majority ethnic group that supports those figures or what comprises those figures across the board? And if so, if -- which ethnic group is it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Based on our information, the information in our possession, which in turn is based on official data, the greatest number of victims across the different categories happen to be Croats, and the percentage is consistently over 80 per cent in all the different categories. Depending on the category, they are followed by Serbs and ethnic Hungarians. But they may -- they are part of the remaining 20 per cent, the Croats accounting for the bulk, the 80 per cent. I can specify in relation to each category, those killed, 88 per cent, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Grujic. But we can look at the report in relation to that information. But one question I'd like to ask you is that in relation to a number of these figures of these groups that we've just discussed, the figure is broken down into defenders, members of civilian protection, civilians, others, and unknown. Now I'm talking in relation to people expelled, killed, detained, missing, et cetera. Can you briefly explain the definition of defender that was used to be able to create that category? Just very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Briefly, defenders are members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And members of the civilian protection, if you can briefly explain who they were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: As an illustration, people like firemen, various council officials, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And -- thank you. And civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Civilians are persons who were in no way involved in the armed combat. Nor could they in any way be linked to any of the armed forces active in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the information that -- as to each individual, whether they fall into a particular category, did that come from the documentation that you had access to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: All the information here is based on documents. All our data were used, and this depended on the completeness of information contained in our questionnaires, based on which we drew up the stats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And regarding the status of a particular victim, whether it be someone that is missing, displaced or detained, or killed, do certain benefits flow from that status in terms of financial benefits to the families of people that have a member killed? And I mean to say: Do different financial benefits flow if someone is categorised as a civilian or a defender?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, there is a distinction there. One thing I have to say, though, is that it is not our place, not up to my administration to determine a person's status or their category. Persons categorised as defenders deserve to be categorised as such because they were members of the armed forces. Of course they have certain entitlements as a result of this. It is in the best interests of every individual who was a member of the armed forces to prove this in order to be able to exercise his entitlements. The entitlements, of course, are of a financial nature. Civilians enjoy no such entitlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Another brief topic about your report, and that's in relation to a statement that you make that exhumation sites -- access was gained to exhumation sites after the liberation of previously occupied areas in the Republic of Croatia. Now, when you state this in your report, are you referring to that area of one-third of Croatia that was occupied as a result of the aggression?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I had in mind. But no access was possible to those areas until such time as they were liberated. Or rather, access was allowed to the Danube area once the peaceful reintegration process was under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And so we can put these figures into context, can you tell us when these areas were liberated from your records and how they were liberated and who liberated them? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: In 1995 the occupied territories were liberated. Eastern Slavonia was the first, while Banovina, Lika and the Croatian south followed. All of this happened in 1995. The peaceful integration process was completed in 1998, as is a generally known fact. And I'm talking about the Danube region now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your records, are you able to say which areas were forcefully liberated and which areas were peacefully liberated?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Of course I can. I signed one of the agreements with UNTAES that involved missing persons. Therefore, I am quite familiar with the areas under UN protection or where the UN forces were operating. I know when they eventually handed over these areas to the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But if you can briefly state which areas were forcefully liberated, by use of force?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The following areas were liberated by the use of force: Western Slavonia, Banovina, Lika and the Croatian south. The Dalmatian hinterland.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And I assume it was the Croatian government forces that liberated those areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, Croatia's legitimate armed forces in a legitimate operation whereby their own territories were liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to those particular territories that were liberated by force, is it fair to say that the ethnic majority in those areas, those occupied areas, was of the Serb group, Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: One could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the forceful liberation of those territories, were any -- were the figures in relation to displaced, killed, detained, were they provided to your office and are they the subject of your report, or does your report largely relate to the aggression and the occupation of Croatia as opposed to the liberation of these occupied areas, in the main?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The information is in relation to the -- or, rather, the consequences of the aggression against the Republic of Croatia. As for the data that you're inquiring about, those in relation to 1995, this information is still being processed, gathered and sorted out. My own office has been cooperating with the neighbouring countries, Serbia and Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a bid to set up a database. I can only provide approximations if I tell you about any information in the possession of my office right now. That is part of the reason why we were involved in the exhumations. This was pursuant to a request by the International Criminal Tribunal, and that's why we did that. However, that's not part of my report, because this type of information has not quite been fully sorted yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So just to summarise, the focus of this report is in relation to a conflict in Croatia, the results of the conflict in Croatia between 1991 and 1996, but focusing more specifically on the aggression against the Croatian state and the occupation of those areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Clearly there was no way we could have been in the possession of documents about deaths in the temporarily occupied areas. It is possible that we can organise this type of documentation over the following period and through bilateral talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as a result of this report relating to Croatia-wide generally, were you also asked by the Office of the Prosecutor recently to analyse the effects of the conflict in the areas of Eastern Slavonia specifically and particularly in relation to the same analytical criteria that you've used of missing, killed, detained, expelled and exhumed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as a result of that request, did you supervise and participate in the production of maps and tables dealing with these figures in this Eastern Slavonian area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Organised and participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the sources that were used to compile these tables and maps, which we'll look at shortly, were they the same sources that you used to arrive at the Croatia-wide statistics in relation to the aggression against the State of Croatia, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The same sources and the same criteria were applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, could I draw your attention to the need to watch time, as was discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are picking up the pace in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the same methodology, was that used?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the term "Eastern Slavonia," is that a geographic region as opposed to a political region, political administrative region?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: It's a geographical concept. Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Srijem. My own analysis, the one that has been used here, was carried out based on their administrative borders. The counties encompassing Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and parts of Srijem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many counties is that and what are their names, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: There are two counties in that area. This is clearly stated in my report. This is the Vukovar-Srijem county and the Osijek-Baranja county. Both these counties were partly occupied, and my analysis is in relation to the occupied areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to this county administrative unit of areas, did the county system come in after 1991? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The counties were introduced in 1993. Back in 1991 the term used was municipalities, and there several of those in these respective areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to counties, counties are made up of municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: They are now, but the borders are different in relation to what they used to be back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can ask you to turn to tab 2.2, please. And this is an analysis of the exhumations that have been conducted in Croatia on a county basis. Now, do you have that map in front of you? It's at tab 2.2. It's ERN number 0600-3720. With the B/C/S translation 0600-3764. Now, the only purpose of looking at this map at the moment is to identify the two counties of Osijek-Baranja and Vukovar-Srijem. Do those two counties appear on the far right-hand side of the Croatian map there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's right. They are on the far right. You see the two lozenges sticking up into the air. That's the Vukovar-Srijem county, number of those exhumed. And the Osijek county. And you can see the border between these two because that, too, is marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So your evidence is that it's the occupied areas within these two counties that was the focus of your analysis in relation to the tables on Eastern Slavonia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that, that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will become Exhibit 537.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, if we can turn to tab 2.3, please. This is a document entitled Osijek-Baranja and Vukovar-Srijem county. And the ERN number is 0600-4079. Mr. Grujic, looking at this map, is the purple area the occupied area that you've referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so that is the area of your analysis in relation to the Eastern Slavonian figures?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, also looking at this map you stated that Eastern Slavonia is located within this region, but in -- certainly in relation to the occupied areas, are there parts of those occupied areas that, in fact, don't form part of Eastern Slavonia, geographically speaking; and if that's correct, which parts, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is primarily in relation to Baranja. But it might be more accurate to use the term Podunavlje, the Danube region, because that term encompasses both counties and the occupied area. We can use this as a geographical concept, including Slavonia, Baranja and Srijem. Or we can simply refer to it as Podunavlje, the Danube region, which I think is more appropriate, if you consider the specific area. The important thing, however, is that the analysis was performed in view of the administrative units that the area is made up of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could ask if that map could be placed on the screen, and if the witness could be provided with a pen, please. The ERN number is 0600-4076.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Apparently there's a problem with the e-court system, so if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not in the system, is the problem. It's not with the system, it's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have thousands of pages for this witness, and every one of them is in the e-court system apart from this one. Very unlucky in that regard. I would ask that we place it on the ELMO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, looking at the map that we're referring to on the ELMO or the projector just beside you, could you draw a line reflecting the areas that would not form a part of Eastern Slavonia in that occupied region, please? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: This is Baranja, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can with --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: And this should be Srijem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you could draw a line where the Baranja region commences, briefly, and also where the Srijem region commences, briefly, to identify those regions as well as the Eastern Slavonia region on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: This is Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could just draw a line on the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could do it a little bit darker, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Isn't this in enough maps already? I'm concerned, Mr. Smith, at the timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can make you feel more confident, the last bit of the examination will be going a lot faster than the first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the time for the whole examination is really drawing to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps if we could agree on a half an hour, would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, could you place an A indicating the Baranja region?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could draw a line indicating where the Srijem region commences and indicate that with a B, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. This is not very accurate. You understand this is very difficult to mark accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. No, we understand that it's an approximation. And with a C can you mark the Eastern Slavonian region, please, in the occupied area.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will become Exhibit 538.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, in addition to being requested to provide an analysis of those that were expelled, missing, detained and exhumed in the Eastern Slavonian region, did you also provide analysis, individual analysis in relation to the Osijek-Baranja county, and also in relation to the Vukovar-Srijem county, and also in relation to the Vukovar town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Applying the same criteria and the same method.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can turn to tab 2.1, please. And this is ERN number 0600-3680 to 0600-3681. Is this the table in relation to your analysis of the Danube region which comprises of those two counties? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And again, these figures simply relate to the occupied region, not the unoccupied region of those counties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the occupation of the areas that you refer to, who occupied these areas, from your records, just briefly, in terms of military forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: According to the information contained in the questionnaire, it was the JNA and paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in this table you refer to the number of people expelled, the number of people that were reported missing or still reported missing now, and the number of people detained, as well as the number of people exhumed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say that in relation to these figures the majority of the people expelled have been -- that have been reported missing and exhumed were, in fact, people of Croat ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. This is a percentage that is roughly equivalent to the one at the state level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can now turn to tab 2.4, please. This is -- and this is ERN number 0600-3702. And this is a map which is entitled identified mass graves in the Eastern Slavonian region. Is this a map that you prepared, or your office prepared?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this map was made in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And it identifies all of the places which have been -- mass graves have been found and exhumed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the mass graves that were found and exhumed in Eastern Slavonia as referred to on the map, are you able to say what percentage of those deaths were by natural causes as opposed to violent causes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you this information, but it is quite clear from the documents we have that in every grave violent causes of death were established. All the persons found in the graves died in the same circumstances and at the same time. In some cases, due to the disappearance of soft tissues, when there are no injuries visible on the bones, it is not possible to ascertain the cause of death. It is certain, however, that in each of the graves victims have been found who have been shown to have died of a violent cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to your categories of analysis from the records that you have, when was the time period in which -- or the main time period in which these expulsions, killings, people being reported missing and -- and detained, when was the main time period when these incidents occurred?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: From September 1991 to around March 1992. That was the highest concentration. And then there is a gradual decline until May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And from your records are you able to say which military formations were the cause of these incidents of expulsion, killing, detention?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: According to the questionnaires about prisoners, over 45 per cent of those taken away by force were taken by the JNA. According to the same information, over 25 per cent were taken away by paramilitary formations. Whereas there is no information available for the others as to who it was that forcibly took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this table in relation to the Danube region, which is 0600-3681 to 0600-36 -- sorry, 80 to 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 539, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also seek to tender the map in relation -- entitled identified mass graves of Eastern Slavonia, and the ERN number is 0600-3720.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, you stated that the basis of your analysis in relation to the effects of the conflict in the Eastern Slavonian region was based on the two counties of Vukovar-Srijem and Osijek-Baranja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the results of your analysis in relation to the Danube region, is that a combined, an aggregate of the results of your independent analyses relating to the Osijek-Baranja region and also the Vukovar-Srijem region?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: The Osijek-Baranja and Vukovar-Srijem counties are an integral part of the analysis of the Podunavlje or Danube region. The Danube region is divided into two administrative entities: The Osijek-Baranja and the Vukovar-Srijem counties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I can turn your attention to tab 2.5, please. This is ERN number 0600-3678 to 0600-3679. Is this your analysis in relation to the Osijek-Baranja county?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Does the same pattern emerge in relation to the percentage of Croats being expelled, detained, killed, as -- does the same pattern emerge as it did in your analysis of the Danube region -- of the Danube region, sorry?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The percentages are very similar. They are just 10 per cent lower in the case of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The table will be Exhibit 541, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
